scan.summary: This is the company's own written Emergency Action Plan for the Portland facility, covering alarms, evacuation, headcount, rescue/medical duties and training for 42 employees. Because it is a program the company wrote itself, it is judged against Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule, OAR 437-002-0042 — Oregon runs its own state plan, so the Oregon rule governs, with the federal 1910.38 as its counterpart. It is a solid plan on evacuation and accountability, but it is missing several of the rule's minimum elements, it says nothing about how employees handle a chemical spill inside the building (which matters for a chemical distributor), and it has not been revised since February 2021 despite promising an annual January review.
scan.freshness_note: The plan is five and a half years old (revised February 2021) even though section 6 says the facilities lead reviews it every January. Five or six annual reviews should have happened since. Ask for the current version and the review record; if February 2021 really is the latest text, the employee count, the alarm vendor, the warden roster and the maps all need checking before anyone relies on this.

gaps.title: No named contact for questions about the plan
gaps.description: The plan never gives a name or job title for the person an employee can contact for more information about the plan or their duties under it. "Facilities lead", "incident coordinator" and "receptionist" are roles used in the text but none is offered as the contact, and no person is named.
gaps.fix: Add a short block at the front or end of the plan: name and job title (and phone/extension) of the person responsible for the plan — most likely the facilities lead — as the contact for questions about the plan and about employees' duties under it.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan describes what the alarm means and that pull stations exist, but never says how an employee raises the alarm or calls for help — who pulls the station, who calls 911, who calls the alarm company, what an employee does if they discover a fire, spill or medical emergency.
gaps.fix: Add a section 'Reporting an emergency' stating: pull the nearest manual pull station, call 911 from any phone, then notify the facilities lead/incident coordinator; list internal and external emergency numbers.
gaps.locator: not in the document — belongs before or within section 2 (Alarm system), page 2
gaps.quote: Manual pull stations are located at each exit door.

gaps.title: No procedure for shutting down critical equipment before evacuating
gaps.description: The plan tells everyone to leave and to "secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds". It does not say which operations must be shut down or made safe first — for example a transfer or filling operation in progress, a lab hood or reaction, a forklift charger — or who stays to do it and when they then leave. The one shutdown named (building ventilation) belongs to shelter-in-place, not to evacuation.
gaps.fix: Add a short subsection to section 3 listing the critical shutdowns (product transfer pumps, lab equipment, ventilation as applicable), the job title responsible for each, and the point at which that person must evacuate regardless.
gaps.quote: When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit.

gaps.title: No chemical spill or release response procedure
gaps.description: For a chemical distributor this is the largest hole. The plan covers an outdoor release (shelter in place) and first aid for someone exposed, but never says what employees do about a spill inside the warehouse or lab: whether anyone may contain or clean up a release, at what size, with what equipment and training, or whether all employees simply evacuate and leave it to the fire department.
gaps.fix: Decide and write down the company's posture: either (a) employees evacuate and outside responders handle all releases — which is the option that lets an emergency action plan stand in place of a full emergency response plan — or (b) named trained employees may respond, which pulls in HAZWOPER responder training levels. State it explicitly and train to it.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(1), adopted in Oregon by OAR 437-002-0100(18) — I have confirmed that Oregon OSHA adopts 1910.120 by reference at 437-002-0100(18); the subsection lettering (q)(1) is the federal text as adopted, and 1910.120(q)(1) allows an employer whose employees evacuate to use an emergency action plan instead
gaps.locator: not in the document — section 3 mentions only outdoor releases
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds.

gaps.title: Appendices A and B are referenced but not in the file
gaps.description: Section 3 and the end of the plan point to Appendix A (evacuation maps) and Appendix B (floor warden and first-aid responder roster). Neither is attached to the PDF, so the exit route assignments and the names of the people with duties under the plan cannot be checked.
gaps.fix: Attach the current maps and the current roster to the plan file, dated, and keep the posted copies matching.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(a) and (2)(e) (Oregon OSHA) — evacuation and exit route assignments, and rescue/medical duties; counterpart to 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(2) and (c)(5)
gaps.quote: Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)

gaps.title: No revision history or record of the annual January reviews
gaps.description: The plan commits to a January review by the facilities lead but carries no revision table, no reviewer signature and no record that any review since February 2021 took place.
gaps.fix: Add a revision history table (date, reviewer, what changed) at the front of the plan and back-fill it from whatever review evidence exists.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

gaps.title: No external spill notification step (OERS)
gaps.description: Nothing in the plan tells anyone to notify the state after a reportable spill or release. In Oregon a spill or release of oil or hazardous material at or above a reportable quantity, or a threatened release, must be reported immediately to the Oregon Emergency Response System on 1-800-452-0311. For a chemical distributor storing packaged product this is a live obligation and the plan is where staff will look for the number.
gaps.fix: Add a short paragraph naming the job title responsible for the notification decision, the OERS number 1-800-452-0311, the National Response Center as applicable, and a pointer to the reportable-quantity rule. Note the containment exception (fully contained, cleaned up within 24 hours, cause repaired).
gaps.citation: OAR 340-142-0040 (Oregon DEQ) — Required Reporting; reportable quantities at OAR 340-142-0050
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds.

gaps.title: Plan is silent on whether employees may fight an incipient fire
gaps.description: The plan says employees evacuate and do not attempt rescue, but never says whether an employee may use a portable fire extinguisher on a small fire on the way out. That choice decides whether extinguisher training obligations apply to all employees or to nobody.
gaps.fix: Add one line to section 3 stating the company's position — either total evacuation with no extinguisher use, or use of extinguishers by designated trained employees only — and match the training in section 6 to it.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0187 (Oregon OSHA, Portable Fire Extinguishers — Oregon's rule in place of 29 CFR 1910.157). I am confident this is the correct Oregon rule number for portable extinguishers; confirm the specific training subsection before drafting to it.
gaps.locator: not in the document — section 3 or section 5
gaps.quote: Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building.

gaps.fix: Name an alternate job title for each role in the plan, and confirm the roster covers every shift that works on site.

scan.confidence_notes: High confidence on what the document is, who it belongs to, and every quote and fact above — they are read directly off pages 1–5. High confidence that Oregon OSHA's own rule OAR 437-002-0042 governs this plan rather than 29 CFR 1910.38 directly, and that its minimum elements at (2) include evacuation procedures, accounting for employees, reporting a fire or other emergency, and shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation — I confirmed that text. Medium confidence on the exact sub-letters (2)(e) and (2)(f) for rescue/medical duties and the named contact; the federal counterparts 1910.38(c)(5) and (c)(6) are certain, the Oregon lettering I have carried forward from the earlier reading and did not verify letter by letter. The earlier reading's uncertainty about the HAZWOPER citation is now resolved on one half: Oregon OSHA adopts 29 CFR 1910.120 by reference at OAR 437-002-0100(18), so cite it as 1910.120(q)(1) as adopted by OAR 437-002-0100(18). The OERS spill reporting rule (OAR 340-142-0040, with quantities at 340-142-0050) I verified. The portable fire extinguisher rule number 437-002-0187 I am confident of as the Oregon rule, but I did not read its training subsection. The document date is only a month and year; I rendered it as the first of the month. The 2026-10-05 alarm test date is my calculation from "first Monday of each month", not a date in the file. The last gap (no named alternates) is inferred, not read. I have not judged whether the plan's contents are true in practice — only what the text does and does not say.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
